title: I-ness (2.6)
hook: the second affliction hides in one tiny Sanskrit word, iva, 'as if'

segments.voice: Yesterday: avidya, ignorance, the passing taken for the permanent and the not-self taken for the self. Did you whisper passing at something that felt like forever? Today, what grows first from that soil. Day four hundred fifty.

Put on a pair of rose-tinted glasses and, after a few minutes, you stop noticing them. The world just looks rosy. Ask yourself what color the sky is, and you'll say pink, and mean it. You're not lying. You've simply forgotten there's anything between your eyes and the sky. The glasses have become part of how you see, and then, without your noticing, part of who you think you are. Sutra 2.6 is about that forgetting.
screen: `ROSE-TINTED GLASSES.` → `THE SKY IS PINK.` → `YOU FORGET THE GLASSES.`

segments.voice: Sutra 2.6: drig darshana shaktyor ekatmata iva asmita. I-ness is when the power of seeing and the instrument of seeing seem to be one self. Drig, the seer: pure awareness, the purusha you met on day four hundred thirty-one. Darshana shakti, the power of seeing, here meaning the instrument, the mind, through which the seer sees. Ekatmata, one-self-ness. And then the small, crucial word: iva, as if. They are not one. They only seem to be. Asmita comes from asmi, I am. It's the felt sense of me: this body, these thoughts, these moods, my story, all bundled together and taken to be the one who sees. Like the glasses and the eyes, fused. Notice the order of the afflictions. First the mistake, ignorance. Then, from it, the mistaken me. That me is what will want things tomorrow and fear things the day after. Asmita isn't the same as arrogance. A shy person has just as much of it as a loud one. It's the basic glue that sticks awareness to the mind's contents. You may remember the same word from chapter one, in the subtlest stage of samadhi with seed: the bare sense of I am. There it was the finest object of absorption. Here it's shown as a knot. The commentators work with both meanings, and they don't contradict: the sense of I am is subtle, and it still isn't the seer.
screen: `DRIG: THE SEER. DARSHANA: THE INSTRUMENT.` · `IVA: AS IF.` · `NOT ARROGANCE: THE GLUE.` · then, large: `THE GLASSES TAKEN FOR THE EYES.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Say silently, I am. Notice what comes with it: maybe a feeling in the chest, a picture of your face, a name, a role. Now notice that you are aware of all of that. The feeling, the picture, the name, all seen. Gently ask: is the one who sees them one more thing on the list? You don't need an answer. Just let the question loosen the glue a little. The bell holds the time.
I-ness. Asmita, sutra 2.6: the seer and the mind it sees through seem to be one self. Seem, as if, iva, is the key.
Your line: asmita. Today, when you catch yourself saying I am, tired, annoyed, behind, try saying I notice, tired, annoyed, behind, and feel the gap. Day four hundred fifty.

howItsDone: In classical yoga, asmita is loosened through discernment between the seer and the seen, and many teachers have students notice the difference between awareness and the thoughts and roles it is aware of.

pairs: the instrument of seeing, the mind

myth: asmita is just another word for arrogance
a shy person has as much as a loud one. it's the glue that sticks awareness to the mind.
the word iva in 2.6 means 'as if'
the seer and the mind only seem to be one.
asmita also appears in chapter one
as the subtlest stage of samadhi with seed, the bare sense of I am (1.17).

fork.setup: you say 'I am anxious.' according to 2.6, what's happening?
options: the seer has truly become anxiety.
the seer and the mind's state seem fused, as if one.
fork.reveal: ekatmata iva: as if one. the mind is anxious; the seer only seems to be.

original.note: Sanskrit asmitā: I-ness, from asmi, 'I am'. the second of the five afflictions.

trapdoor: what you thought: I-ness means selfishness.
what it means: the seeming fusion of awareness with the mind it sees through.
what a scholar hears: 2.6 hinges on iva ('as if'); asmita is also the subtlest support of samprajnata samadhi in 1.17, so the same word names both a knot and a fine object of absorption.

sources.ref: Yoga Sutras of Patanjali 1.17 (asmita in samadhi with seed)

notes: Darshana-shakti rendered 'the instrument of seeing (the mind/buddhi)'; translations vary ('power of seeing'). Confirm.
The relation between asmita in 1.17 and in 2.6 is explained without ranking interpretations; confirm framing.
Rose-tinted glasses image is the writer's.
